Basal metabolic rate in Sigmodon alleni was assessed via respirometry under controlled laboratory conditions. At a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], resting oxygen consumption reached a maximum of 194.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 194.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the moderate energetic demands typical of a medium-sized cricetid rodent. This metabolic ceiling provides a physiological baseline for understanding the species' overall energy budget and its capacity for sustained activity in the seasonally dry tropical forests of western Mexico where it is endemic.

Reproductive output in this species is limited by a very low annual frequency. Females produce a maximum of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], and litter sizes range from two to six pups [N_R_i = two to six pups], yielding a modest annual fecundity that likely reflects constraints imposed by a prolonged period of maternal investment. All reproductive data reported here were collected from individuals maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the standard thermoneutral temperature for this species.

Birth mass in Sigmodon alleni is estimated indirectly using data from its congener Sigmodon hispidus, which suggests a neonatal wet weight of 6.2 grams [Wwb = 6.2 grams]. This relatively small size at parturition is typical of altricial rodents that undergo a significant period of post-natal development within the nest. The altricial neonate is entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition during the first week of life, a phase that imposes substantial energetic costs on the lactating female.

Adult body size in Sigmodon alleni exhibits a slight but consistent sexual dimorphism. Females attain a maximum adult wet weight of 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], while males reach a slightly lower ultimate body mass of 178 grams [Wwi = 178 grams]. This pattern, where females are marginally heavier than males, is uncommon among polygynous rodents but has been documented in several other grassland-inhabiting sigmodontines and may be linked to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.
